purpose: Mechlorethamine is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain cancers, including Hodgkin lymphoma and a skin condition called mycosis fungoides (a type of skin lymphoma). It works by slowing down or stopping the growth of cancer cells. The gel form is applied directly to the skin, while the injection form is given through a vein in a hospital or clinic setting.
how_it_works: Mechlorethamine works by attaching itself to the DNA inside cancer cells, which prevents those cells from being able to copy themselves and grow. Think of it like putting a lock on the cancer cell's instruction manual so it can't make more copies. Because it targets fast-growing cells, it is very effective at fighting cancer, though it can also affect some healthy cells in the body.
common_side_effects: Skin redness, itching, rash, or darkening of the skin (especially with the gel form). With the injection, you may experience nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, mouth sores, hair loss, or low blood cell counts which can lead to fatigue or increased risk of infection.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your blood cell counts, increasing the risk of infections, bleeding, and anemia — tell your doctor right away if you have a fever or unusual bruising. It can harm an unborn baby, so reliable birth control is very important during treatment. Avoid getting the gel in your eyes or mouth. Let your healthcare team know about all other medications you take, as interactions are possible. This medicine is also a known carcinogen with long-term use.
typical_dosing: For the skin gel (Valchlor 0.016%): it is usually applied once a day to affected areas of the skin. For the injection (Mustargen): the dose is calculated based on your body weight and type of cancer, and it is given by a healthcare professional, often as part of a combination chemotherapy regimen. Your doctor will determine the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
